labels.swarmItem: Area: MessagePack serializer. Slugs: fuzz_msgpacker_encode_scalars, fuzz_msgpacker_decode_scalars, fuzz_msgpacker_blobs, fuzz_msgpacker_arrays, fuzz_msgpacker_dicts. Only source file you may modify: /workspace/fuzz/msgpacker.py. Implement every TODO method in the encoder and decoder classes per their docstrings (MessagePack wire format: fixint/uint8-64/int8-64, bool 0xc2/0xc3, nil 0xc0, fixstr/str8/str16/str32, bin8/16/32, fixarray/array16/32, fixmap/map16/32) plus the encode() and decode() dispatchers. /workspace/fuzz/msgpacker_example.py shows usage. There is no grader.py in fuzz/ — verify with thorough round-trip tests of your own (scalars at format boundaries like 127/128/255/256/65535, -32/-33, strings/bytes at 31/32/255/256 chars, nested arrays/dicts, tuples decoding to tuples per the decode_array docstring). If the `msgpack` pip package is installed you may cross-check against it, but msgpacker.py itself must not depend on it.

Area: Printable Codec. Slugs: fuzz_codec_encode, fuzz_codec_decode. Only source file you may modify: /workspace/fuzz/codec.py. Implement encode(input) so ASCII letters and digits pass through unchanged and every other byte becomes an uppercase %XX escape (3 printable ASCII bytes); implement decode(buf) to reverse percent escapes and silently drop truncated partial escapes at the ends (see the docstrings and requirements comment block in the file). Check /workspace/fuzz/Makefile for how the codec is exercised.

Area: ECDSA bad-random attacks. Slugs: ecdsa_timestamp_key, ecdsa_nonce_reuse. Only source file you may modify: /workspace/bad-random/ecdsa/sol.py. Read /workspace/bad-random/ecdsa/grader.py and keygen.py first. problem_1a(date_string, public_key): brute-force every Unix timestamp on the given calendar day, derive the candidate secret exponent with SHA-256 exactly as keygen.py does, and return the SigningKey whose verifying key matches public_key. problem_2b(sig1, sig2, Hm1, Hm2): recover the private scalar from two ECDSA signatures that reused the same nonce k (standard nonce-reuse algebra mod the curve order; read the grader/keygen for curve and signature tuple format). The `ecdsa` pip package is likely missing — install it. Run grader.py until it passes; note in your report how long the brute force takes.

Area: WEP packet forgery. Slugs: wep_known_plaintext_forgery, wep_xor_mask_forgery. Only source file you may modify: /workspace/bad-random/wep/attacker.py. Read /workspace/bad-random/wep/victim.py and grader.py first. attack_one(plaintext, ciphertext, attack_msg): recover the RC4 keystream from the known pair (mind the IV bytes and CRC32 trailer layout) and forge a packet that decrypts to attack_msg with a valid CRC32. attack_two(ciphertext, attack_msg): without knowing the plaintext, forge a packet that decrypts to (original plaintext XOR attack_msg mask) while keeping the CRC32 trailer valid, exploiting CRC32 linearity (you may need a GF(2) CRC32 delta function — pure Python is fine). Run grader.py until both grade_one and grade_two pass.

Area: Python escape attacks. Slugs: escape_closure_secret (attack_one), escape_stack_secret (attack_two), escape_random_control (attack_three), escape_gc_secret (attack_four). Only source file you may modify: /workspace/escape/attack.py. Read /workspace/escape/grader.py very carefully — it defines the four scenarios and exactly what is checked. attack_one(guess): recover the bytes secret captured by the equality-oracle closure (introspect the function's __closure__ cells). attack_two(): walk caller frames (sys._getframe) to recover the caller local named `secret`. attack_three(): hijack os.urandom so the NEXT bytes the caller obtains from os.urandom are attacker-controlled (read the grader to see how it verifies control; ctypes or gc-based patching may be needed depending on how the grader holds the reference). attack_four(): recover a bytes secret from a cyclic object still reachable through the garbage collector (gc.get_objects / get_referrers). Interpreter is CPython 3.11. Run grader.py until all four scenarios pass.

Area: WebAssembly SHA-256 sandbox. Slug: wasm_sandbox. Only source file you may modify: /workspace/wasm/sandbox.py. Read /workspace/wasm/grader.py, wasi.py, requirements.txt, Makefile, and sha.c to understand how sha-export.wasm was built and what the sandbox must do. Implement sha256(v: bytes) -> bytes: load /workspace/wasm/sha-export.wasm using the wasmtime Python package (install per requirements.txt if missing), instantiate it with any WASI/import wiring the module needs (reuse wasi.py if the grader does), write the input bytes into wasm linear memory, invoke the exported SHA256 function, and copy the 32-byte digest back out. Verify correctness against hashlib.sha256 for several inputs and run the grader until it passes.

Area: Merkle tree (largest area). Slugs: merkle_common, merkle_store_lookup, merkle_store_insert, merkle_client_lookup, merkle_client_insert, merkle_attack_one, merkle_attack_two, merkle_attack_three, merkle_attack_four. Only source files you may modify: /workspace/merkle/common.py, /workspace/merkle/store.py, /workspace/merkle/client.py, /workspace/merkle/attack.py. Read /workspace/merkle/grader.py first — it defines every scenario — plus server.py, cli.py, and /workspace/docs/lab5.md (the lab handout) for the intended design. Implement: common.py (H, H_empty, H_kv, H_internal, traversal_path); store.py (traversal direction tracking, node traversal on empty/leaf/internal nodes, proof construction, Store.lookup, InsertTraversal.leaf, Store.insert with overwrites); client.py (validate, lookup, insert recomputing the root and handling overwrites/forks); attack.py (AttackOne/Two/Three/Four helpers as exercised by the grader). Run grader.py until all scenarios pass. In your report, map each of the 9 slugs to the specific functions that implement it.

lastPrompt: This task is based on an undergraduate computer-security lab sequence. You will implement a set of security-related units covering encoding, serialization, cryptographic attacks, Merkle-tree proofs, Python escape attacks, and a WebAssembly sandbox wrapper. Your working directory is `/workspace`. The project code is already present. You need to implement the units below so that all tests pass. Implement the following units: Printable Codec (`fuzz/codec.py`): `fuzz_codec_encode`: implement `encode(input)` so ASCII letters and digits pass through and all other bytes become uppercase `%XX` escapes. `fuzz_codec_decode`: implement `decode(buf)` so it reverses percent escapes and drops truncated trailing escapes. MessagePack Serializer (`fuzz/msgpacker.py`): `fuzz_msgpacker_encode_scalars`: implement scalar encoding and encode dispatch for ints, bools, and `None`. `fuzz_msgpacker_decode_scalars`: implement scalar decoding and decode dispatch for ints, bools, and `None`. `fuzz_msgpacker_blobs`: implement string and bytes encoding/decoding. `fuzz_msgpacker_arrays`: implement array encoding/decoding. `fuzz_msgpacker_dicts`: implement dict encoding/decoding. ECDSA Attacks (`bad-random/ecdsa/sol.py`): `ecdsa_timestamp_key`: recover the signing key by brute-forcing all timestamps on the given date. `ecdsa_nonce_reuse`: recover the private scalar from two signatures that reused the same nonce. WEP Packet Forgery (`bad-random/wep/attacker.py`): `wep_known_plaintext_forgery`: forge an attacker-chosen message from a known plaintext/ciphertext pair. `wep_xor_mask_forgery`: xor an unknown plaintext by an attacker-chosen mask while fixing CRC32. Python Escape Attacks (`escape/attack.py`): `escape_closure_secret`: recover a bytes secret from a closure-backed equality oracle. `escape_stack_secret`: recover the caller local secret from the Python frame stack. `escape_random_control`: control the next bytes returned by `os.urandom`. `escape_gc_secret`: recover a bytes secret from a cyclic object still reachable through the garbage collector. WebAssembly SHA-256 Sandbox (`wasm/sandbox.py`): `wasm_sandbox`: load `sha-export.wasm`, allocate memory, invoke the exported `SHA256`, and return the 32-byte digest. Merkle Tree Hashes (`merkle/common.py`): `merkle_common`: implement `H`, `H_empty`, `H_kv`, `H_internal`, and `traversal_path`. Merkle Tree Store (`merkle/store.py`): `merkle_store_lookup`: implement the traversal helpers and proof construction needed for lookups. `merkle_store_insert`: implement insertion traversal, overwrites, and `Store.insert()`. Merkle Tree Client (`merkle/client.py`): `merkle_client_lookup`: implement proof validation and `lookup()`. `merkle_client_insert`: implement `insert()` so the client recomputes the correct root hash after updates. Merkle Tree Attacks (`merkle/attack.py`): `merkle_attack_one`: implement the AttackOne helpers. `merkle_attack_two`: implement the AttackTwo helpers. `merkle_attack_three`: implement the AttackThree lookup behavior. `merkle_attack_four`: implement the AttackFour helpers. The tests also depend on these signatures and entry points: fuzz/codec.py: `encode(input: bytes) -> bytes` `decode(buf: bytes) -> bytes` bad-random/ecdsa/sol.py: `problem_1a(date_string: str, public_key) -> SigningKey` `problem_2b(sig1: tuple, sig2: tuple, Hm1: int, Hm2: int) -> int` bad-random/wep/attacker.py: `Attacker.attack_one(plaintext: bytes, ciphertext: bytes, attack_msg: bytes) -> bytes` `Attacker.attack_two(ciphertext: bytes, attack_msg: bytes) -> bytes` escape/attack.py: `attack_one(guess) -> bytes` `attack_two() -> bytes` `attack_three() -> bytes` `attack_four() -> bytes` wasm/sandbox.py: `sha256(v: bytes) -> bytes` You are running as a long-horizon autonomous engineering agent at `/workspace`. This task spans many files and requirements, and is expected to take many iterations. Read every requirement under `/workspace/requirements/` (and any other explicit requirement list referenced by the task) and only finish
